Daniel is essentially describing “projector–camera” closed-loop compensation, but the post slides past the hardest constraint: the system is optimizing *what the camera sees*, not what a human perceives. Once the wall is colored, textured, glossy, or 3D, you run into radiometric and geometric limits—camera/projector dynamic range, non-Lambertian reflections, ambient light, and occlusions—that no amount of feedback can fully invert. The classic work here frames the problem less as generic control and more as calibration + per-pixel radiometric compensation (often GPU-shader-based), with feedback mainly used to track drift rather than continuously “optimize” an unconstrained objective; see [Shader Lamps](https://web.media.mit.edu/~raskar/tr/ShaderLamps/) and broader projector–camera literature (e.g., [Ramesh Raskar](https://web.media.mit.edu/~raskar/), [Shree Nayar](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~nayar/)). Naming that lineage would clarify what is known to work reliably (moderate surface variation, controlled lighting) versus what tends to fail (highly specular/complex geometry, large viewpoint changes).

The “camera near the (one) viewer’s eyes” line is also a pivotal assumption that deserves more explicit treatment: it turns the system into a single-user, viewpoint-dependent display. That can be a feature—effectively a personal “corrected” projection mapped to one eye point—but it won’t generalize to multiple viewers without either sacrificing correction quality or adding more cameras/view-dependent rendering. There’s also a practical control issue: low latency matters more than people expect. If the viewer moves and the loop lags, you get swimming distortions that feel worse than an uncorrected projection; this is why many systems separate fast head-pose tracking (predictive) from slower photometric recalibration.

Finally, the face-detection “blacken the region” safety idea is morally sensible but technically underspecified. First, it’s not just faces—eyes can be exposed at angles where detection is unreliable, and failures are worst-case. Second, “blackening” can still be bright if the projector’s black level is elevated by ambient light or if the wall reflects strongly. In practice, safety is usually handled with optical design (throw angle, lens hooding, physical barriers), conservative brightness limits, and standards-aware operation, with vision-based masking as a supplementary layer—not the primary guarantee. It’s also worth noting the privacy dimension: a system that continuously captures a room to protect people is still a surveillance camera unless Daniel explicitly constrains storage/processing and communicates that boundary.
